meta.title: GPT-6.1 Sol · Biology · solo · run 1
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 37 of 51 credited claims; 14 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Leakage-controlled structured transfer predicts TEM-1 Firnberg fitness
artifacts.summary: Combines target-assay biochemical regression, low-rank and saturating latent models with cross-fitted predictors from the Stiffler assay. The frozen release was evaluated on five fresh random mutation holdouts after exploratory selection. Reported MAE is pooled across splits; uncertainty resamples positions, preserving within-position dependence. Repeated validation splits are not independent experimental replicates. The local ridge implementation was checked against the supplied sequence-one-hot comparator. For paired assays, all queried mutations are removed from the source before constructing any source predictor; source features and target-model stacking are cross-fitted within training. Scope: missing substitutions within these assays, mainly at partially observed positions; no unseen-protein or unseen-position claim.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0942, 95% CI [-0.1037, -0.0844], beyond the minimum effect 0.0046)

claim.statement: The released predictor reduces DMS-score mean absolute error relative to the supplied one-hot sequence ridge comparator on held-out single substitutions in this assay.

artifacts.title: Cross-fitted local tolerance profiles outperform structured completion for TEM-1 Firnberg
artifacts.summary: The profile learner uses only the target assay. Its features include the observed same-position score distribution, chemical-neighbor weighted predictions, regularized position-wise chemical fits, amino-acid-group summaries, and global substitution means. A structured predictor is included as a cross-fitted feature. Training features are generated out of fold; query features never read query targets. The comparison arm is the same structured predictor alone, not the weaker supplied ridge baseline. The learner and parameters were frozen before these fresh validation splits. Position-block bootstrap intervals capture within-position dependence; repeated splits are not independent experiments. The claim concerns interpolation of missing substitutions, not entirely unmeasured positions.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm a beats the other arm (difference -0.0282, 95% CI [-0.0325, -0.0239], beyond the minimum effect 0.0032)

claim.statement: A cross-fitted nonlinear learner on local mutational tolerance profiles improves held-out single-substitution MAE over the released structured biochemical/low-rank predictor alone.

artifacts.title: Untyped sequence smoothing outperforms amino-acid-selective smoothing in sparse CASP3
artifacts.summary: Matched positive-semidefinite kernel comparison. Both arms contain position identity, mutant identity, wild-type/mutant identity, and within-position biochemical similarity with identical weights and regularization. Arm a adds exponential sequence-distance covariance multiplied by an RBF similarity of mutant amino-acid physicochemical descriptors; arm b adds the same sequence-distance covariance without mutant similarity. Thus only the sequence-local sharing assumption differs. All assays and both directions were inspected; the reported direction is assay-specific, not a universal advantage. The CASP3 result may reflect sparse per-position coverage or model misspecification and does not establish a biological mechanism.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm b beats the other arm (difference -0.0242, 95% CI [-0.0398, -0.0084], beyond the minimum effect 0.0081)

claim.statement: At the fixed matched kernel settings, sequence-local sharing without amino-acid selectivity yields lower held-out CASP3 MAE than amino-acid-selective sharing.

artifacts.title: A saturating response link improves matched latent completion for TEM-1 Firnberg
artifacts.summary: Matched comparison between rank-three latent position-by-mutant models with identical regularization, pseudo-Huber loss, and optimizer budget. Arm a maps its latent score through a sigmoid with endpoints estimated solely from training-score quantiles; arm b uses a linear response link. Fresh random mutation holdouts confirm the direction selected in exploratory experiments. Position-block bootstrap intervals preserve within-position dependence. This is a predictive model comparison, not identification of a biological mechanism or a claim that the saturating model is the best available predictor.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm a beats the other arm (difference -0.0127, 95% CI [-0.0177, -0.0076], beyond the minimum effect 0.0032)

claim.statement: A saturating response link reduces held-out mutation MAE compared with a linear link in the fixed matched robust latent-factor model.

artifacts.title: Biochemical profile summaries outperform raw amino-acid profiles for TEM-1 Firnberg
artifacts.summary: Matched gradient-boosted learners receive identical mutation descriptors, local tolerance moments, and global mutant/substitution summaries. Arm a augments these with biochemical and BLOSUM-weighted interpolation, regularized local chemical coefficients, and residue-class summaries; arm b instead receives all observed same-position amino-acid scores, centered scores, and observation masks. Training features are generated in held-out folds, and every query substitution is excluded from its own profile. Fresh mutation holdouts and position-block bootstrap intervals support this algorithm-specific inductive-bias comparison. This does not claim biochemical summaries contain more information than raw profiles or identify a causal mechanism. No source assay is used.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm a beats the other arm (difference -0.0107, 95% CI [-0.0154, -0.0061], beyond the minimum effect 0.0030)

claim.statement: With the fixed cross-fitted learner, biochemical profile summaries reduce held-out mutation MAE relative to raw amino-acid profile features.

artifacts.title: Paired-assay profiles improve position-masked prediction for TEM-1 Firnberg
artifacts.summary: An explicit masking protocol removes all target-assay observations in the query position group before fitting either arm. Position groups are deterministic and independent of labels. Arm b is a target-only structured predictor; arm a is a meta-learner using cross-fitted source-assay position statistics and completion predictions plus target-only predictions, trained with position-group cross-fitting. Every queried mutation is removed from the paired source assay globally before feature construction; other source-assay substitutions at those positions remain available. Thus this tests target-position extrapolation conditional on a partially measured paired assay, not unseen-protein generalization. The released comparison applies this masking even when the evaluator supplies target training observations at query positions. Validation uses fresh mutation holdouts under exactly that masking protocol. Intervals resample positions; repeated splits are not independent biological replicates.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm a beats the other arm (difference -0.2332, 95% CI [-0.2464, -0.2196], beyond the minimum effect 0.0075)

claim.statement: Under the released target-position masking protocol, paired-assay profile transfer reduces held-out MAE relative to target-only structured prediction.

artifacts.title: Profile-stacked release improves held-out prediction for TEM-1 Firnberg
artifacts.summary: Upgraded release of the structured predictor. Most weight is placed on cross-fitted biochemical tolerance-profile learners, with a smaller complementary structured/sequence-context ensemble. Every queried mutation is globally excluded from the paired source assay before source predictors are constructed; training meta-features are cross-fitted. A frozen release was tested on fresh random mutation holdouts, followed by target-free inference and row-permutation audits. Reported pooled error intervals resample positions; overlapping splits are not independent biological replicates. The earlier structured-only release remains available as historical evidence, but this code is the recommended prediction release. Scope: held-out substitutions within these assays, not unseen proteins. Baseline comparison does not isolate the effect of cross-assay transfer.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0982, 95% CI [-0.1080, -0.0882], beyond the minimum effect 0.0046)

claim.statement: The released cross-fitted profile-stacked predictor reduces held-out DMS-score MAE relative to the supplied sequence-one-hot ridge baseline.

artifacts.title: Paired-assay transfer helps sparse-target prediction for TEM-1 Firnberg
artifacts.summary: Both arms use the same deterministic label-independent target-assay subsample and identical cross-fitted profile learners. The retained target observations are selected by a fixed hash of mutation identity; arm a additionally receives paired-assay position summaries and completion predictions. Every evaluation mutation is removed globally from the paired assay, and meta-training source features are fold-excluded. This tests transfer in the sparse-target regime conditional on an available paired assay, not a comparison against unrestricted target-data training. The released test applies the same subsampling to both arms. Full-data controls show substantially smaller gains, so this result must not be generalized to dense target assays.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm a beats the other arm (difference -0.0423, 95% CI [-0.0512, -0.0339], beyond the minimum effect 0.0036)

claim.statement: Under the released sparse-target subsampling protocol, paired-assay profile features reduce held-out mutation MAE relative to the same target-only learner.

artifacts.title: Biochemical sequence smoothing improves position-masked KCNE1 expression
artifacts.summary: Both arms remove every target-assay observation in each query position group using a fixed label-independent grouping. Both use identical position, mutant, substitution, and position-chemical kernels. Arm a adds a sequence-distance kernel multiplied by amino-acid chemical similarity; arm b adds the same sequence-distance kernel without amino-acid specificity. No paired assay is used. Fresh split confirmation includes a third control without either sequence-smoothing term. Thus the finding concerns predictive inductive bias for unmeasured positions within KCNE1, not unseen proteins or a causal account of membrane topology. Position-block bootstrap intervals condition on this protein and fixed grouping.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm a beats the other arm (difference -0.0192, 95% CI [-0.0312, -0.0072], beyond the minimum effect 0.0051)

artifacts.title: Other-protein response kernels improve matched interpolation for CASP3 activity
artifacts.summary: A simple kernel regressor combines position, mutant identity, substitution identity, and position-specific amino-acid response similarity. Arm a learns the response covariance from other protein families; arm b uses fixed physicochemical and BLOSUM embeddings. Both arms average centered/raw covariance variants and use identical kernel weights and ridge penalties. All assays from the target protein family are excluded from external covariance estimation, so paired-assay transfer cannot explain the result. Fresh random-mutation split confirmation and position-block bootstrap intervals are reported. This isolates a useful transferable response prior in a simple model; it does not claim superiority over the richer released profile-stacked predictor. Improvement is assay-dependent and was not universal in the initial all-assay screen.

artifacts.title: KCNE1 expression smoothing benefit survives contiguous position-block masking
artifacts.summary: Robustness extension of the interleaved position-mask result. Both arms now remove complete contiguous sequence blocks from target-assay training, according to the released fixed label-independent grouping. artifacts.title: Reproducibility report and scope qualifications for released DMS predictors
artifacts.summary: Consolidated report of recorded comparisons, leakage audits, evaluator-interface smoke tests, and limitations. The profile-stacked prediction release is the recommended practical predictor; matched ablations isolate modeling choices. KCNE1-function position smoothing remains tentative because its position-bootstrap interval includes no benefit and its contiguous-block extension failed; KCNE1 expression is the robust smoothing finding. Clarification for direct covariance artifacts: the external arm averages raw and position-centered response covariances, whereas the fixed arm averages physicochemical and BLOSUM covariances. Sparse-target comparisons use the same restricted target subsample in both arms and do not establish superiority over full-target-data training. REPORT.md is attached as a blob.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publication rules, then choose a tractable question with a credible held-out test.
I’ll inspect the splits and baseline models before choosing a target, paying particular attention to transfer between assays of the same protein.
The initial output was truncated. I’ll read the baseline and data format separately so the validation design matches the evaluator’s setup.

The comparator cannot model position-specific substitution chemistry. I’ll test whether shared substitution patterns and measurements from a paired assay improve prediction, using target labels held out from training.
I’ll start with a common validation screen across all assays: compare one-hot ridge against substitution-aware regression, low-rank completion, and nonlinear biochemical models.
The screen failed to import its local module. I’ll inspect the execution directory and Python path before retrying.
The runner excludes the working directory from Python’s import path. I’ll add it explicitly and rename the audit script so it cannot shadow Python’s standard library.

The first split favors structured models over the baseline on most assays. I’ll now test whether paired assays add information beyond a strong single-assay model, including when the exact source mutation is unavailable.

Transfer looks especially promising between the β-lactamase assays, while the other paired phenotypes need more than a monotone mapping. I’ll test better single-assay models and repeated splits before choosing a final method.
The broader model search is running in the background. I’ll audit mutation coverage and paired-assay overlap to define appropriate controls for the transfer experiments.

The paired assays have almost identical public mutation sets, so direct source lookup makes random target-only validation misleading. I’ll rerun transfer with validation mutations removed from both assays to approximate hidden-mutation prediction.
A joint position-by-amino-acid model could use paired assays without relying on exact mutation lookup. I’ll compare shared low-rank completion with separate fits under synchronized mutation holdout.
I’ll review the synchronized results and verify the baseline implementation. Any final claims will exclude the earlier direct-lookup gains unless they hold under the stricter split.

Synchronized transfer still helps, especially for β-lactamase and KRAS binding. CASP3 has much sparser coverage per position; I’ll test amino-acid similarity kernels that can borrow information between chemically related substitutions.
I’ll check the running searches and identify stable model families rather than selecting a winner from one split.
I’ll prepare a stricter transfer control that cross-fits both assays when constructing training features. It will also separate measured-source effects from source-model effects.
I’ll check the kernel results and summarize the joint-model search. For CASP3, I’m looking for settings that improve prediction consistently across splits.

Joint low-rank completion is not consistently better than the simpler models. I’ll test a different biochemical constraint: using neutral wild-type substitutions as soft anchors in sparse mutation matrices.
I’ll examine a saturating low-rank model while the anchor control runs. Fitness scores can have floor and ceiling effects, which a purely additive model may not capture.
I’ll review the anchor control and check the exact comparator. The aim is to retain models whose gains survive multiple splits without depending on a special score-scale assumption.
The soft-anchor variants rarely beat the current model. I’ll test whether local sequence context and nearby positions provide useful sharing, particularly in the sparsely sampled CASP3 landscape.

I’ll test a model that uses the observed substitutions at each position as a local tolerance profile. Training features will exclude the row’s own label, allowing nonlinear prediction without self-label leakage.
I’ll compare the completed searches using average and worst-split performance. Any selected model will then face new validation splits.

A useful remaining question is whether dense landscapes from other proteins can help sparse CASP3 data. I’ll test shared substitution effects while keeping position effects protein-specific and allowing each assay its own scale.
I’ll review the profile and cross-protein models, then use fresh splits to assess the most promising candidates rather than continuing broad tuning.
I’ll set up a fresh-split confirmation run for the selected model families, including paired-error confidence intervals and position-block bootstrap uncertainty.
The local-profile model may be a simpler way to capture position-by-substitution interactions. I’ll check its results before adding it to the confirmation pipeline.
I’ll inspect runtime and CPU use while confirmation runs. Then I’ll prepare paired-bootstrap summaries and executable publication tests.

I’ll test one more route for sparse-data transfer: learn correlations between substitution effects from the denser landscapes, then use those correlations as a prior for unmeasured CASP3 substitutions.
I’ll review the fresh-split confirmation and profile results. These should show whether nonlinear tolerance profiles generalize beyond the exploratory splits.

Fresh splits confirm gains over ridge across all assays. Transfer helps β-lactamase and KRAS binding, while sequence smoothing looks more useful for KCNE1 expression. I’ll fix the failed covariance control and continue testing local profiles.

I’ll retrieve the confirmation predictions and compute paired uncertainty estimates. The summaries will resample positions so substitutions at the same residue are not treated as independent evidence.
I’ll record the position-bootstrap summary and inspect the profile-model search for any stronger, interpretable improvements.

Local tolerance profiles are competitive with paired-assay transfer on several landscapes. I’ll test a combined model that can use both, then verify the publication interface before freezing the implementation.
I’ll test two ways to make the profile model less sensitive to assay scale: predict a correction to the local mean, or predict a correction to a cross-fitted structured model.
I’ll verify the data documentation and held-out file format, then test categorical-position trees as a compact alternative to the hand-built profile model.
The summary run found no tables, likely because folder blobs are mounted as archives. I’ll make input extraction explicit and rerun it so the uncertainty estimates are actually recorded.
I’ll inspect the combined-model results and fixed bootstrap summaries, then choose a compact final pipeline and meaningful comparison claims.
I’ll inspect the model implementation for indexing or feature-construction errors before relying on it in held-out tests.
I’ll freeze the confirmed pipeline as a reproducible first release and test its inference path with target-free inputs. This gives us a publishable result while the remaining ablations finish.
The release smoke test could not import its local module. I’ll make the module path explicit and rerun it before publishing.
The release smoke test passes. I’ll now run all seven release configurations on fresh splits, so every published test has direct executable evidence.
I’ll compare the profile-transfer and residual ablations. If simpler models perform similarly, I’ll keep the smaller release rather than add complexity.
I’ll prepare a head-to-head comparison of paired transfer against a strong single-assay profile model. This tests whether transfer adds value beyond merely sharing effects across substitutions.

I’ll check the running jobs and publication schema before freezing claims. The main result is already supported by fresh-split validation; the remaining controls test whether paired assays add value over strong single-assay models.

The frozen release beats ridge across all seven assays on fresh splits. I’ll record aggregate metrics and position-bootstrap intervals, then publish assay-specific claims with executable held-out tests.

I’ll publish the frozen release with explicit limits: it predicts missing substitutions at partially observed positions, not unseen proteins or entirely unmeasured sites. Paired-assay inference excludes the queried mutation from the source assay.
